intro.title:
Why does exclusion
hurt?
intro.text: For the brain, social rejection is the same as physical pain. It activates the same areas in the brain. That's why 'don't care' advice doesn't work.

survival.title: Survival Kit
survival.text: When you feel sidelined, try these three steps.

step1.title: 1. Acknowledge the pain
step1.text: Say to yourself: 'This hurts because I am human.' Pain tells you that you need connection.

step2.title: 2. Find connection elsewhere
step2.text: Send a message to a friend. Make eye contact with a cashier. Even a small accepting look relieves pain.

step3.title: 3. Validate yourself
step3.text: Remember a moment when you were appreciated. It is just as true as this moment.

validation.title: Self-Worth Validation

summary.title: Remember this

intro.title: Identify the patterns.
intro.text:
Bullying is not an accident, but often a recurring pattern. In this module, you will learn to distinguish a normal workplace rift from systematic bullying.

🏆 Complete the test at the end to get a certificate mark.

theory_content.item1: Systematic nature: Bullying is not a one-off conflict, but a process lasting weeks or months.
theory_content.item2: Power imbalance: The target has difficulty defending themselves (e.g., manager-subordinate relationship or a group against one).
theory_content.item3: Intentionality: Acts aim to isolate, humiliate, or cause the target to fail at work.

boundaries_module.subtitle: Reclaiming Your Space

intro.title:
Boundaries are not walls.
They are gateways.
intro.text:
In a bullying situation, your boundaries have often been trampled down. For recovery, it's important to learn to say "no" again, so you can say "yes" to your own well-being.

A boundary is not an attack on another, but an act of love toward yourself.

categories_step.title: Which boundary do you need most?

professional.title: Professional Boundaries
professional.description: What you do and when. Limits of responsibility.
examples: I don't respond to emails after 5 PM.
This task is not part of my job description right now.
I need 3 hours of uninterrupted time daily.

emotional.title: Emotional Boundaries
emotional.description: Whose burden you carry and where you spend your energy.
examples: I can't listen to this right now, I don't have the space.
I don't need to explain my decisions to you.
I can discuss this professionally, but I won't accept yelling.

physical.title: Physical & Communication Boundaries
physical.description: Your space, touch, and how you're approached.
examples: I'd prefer we don't use personal channels for work matters.
I'd appreciate if you kept a bit of distance when speaking.

steps.speaker: Narrator
steps.text: You see your colleague Marja being criticized baselessly and sarcastically in a team meeting. Marja looks paralyzed and stares at the table.

choices.text: Move to sit next to Marja and ask quietly: 'Are you okay?'
choices.feedback: Research: Mere physical presence and asking 'Are you okay?' reduces the victim's anxiety by up to 40%.

choices.text: Challenge the bully directly in the meeting: 'Stop that immediately!'
choices.feedback: Direct confrontation can escalate and increase your own risk, although it is brave.

steps.speaker: Marja
steps.text: Marja glances at you gratefully and takes a deep breath. The bully slows down their speech noticing that Marja is no longer alone.

choices.text: Name the situation factually: 'Shall we continue with the agenda? Marja's input was important here.'
choices.feedback: Showing solidarity publicly stabilizes the situation without a fight.

steps.speaker: Narrator
steps.text: The bully turns to you: 'Well look, someone's being sensitive today! Do you have a club going on?' The atmosphere tightens.

choices.text: Stay calm: 'It's about workplace rules, not sensitivity.'
choices.feedback: Calmness is the best weapon when the other party tries to personalize the conflict.

steps.speaker: Narrator
steps.text: The meeting ends. Marja comes to thank you later. She says that without your support she might have burst into tears or left the room.

choices.text: Finish exercise
choices.feedback: Great! You are an active witness breaking the cycle of isolation.

steps.speaker: WhatsApp Group
steps.text: Mocking memes about the newest hobbyist start spreading in the group. No one comments anything, although 20 people have seen the messages.

choices.text: Write in the group: 'This doesn't belong here, do others agree?'
choices.feedback: By asking for others' opinion, you break 'pluralistic ignorance' and share responsibility.

choices.text: Leave the group in silence
choices.feedback: Leaving is a sign, but it leaves the victim alone. Try intervening in the group.

steps.speaker: Narrator
steps.text: It's quiet for a moment, but then two other members thumbs-up your message and write: 'True, let's stick to the topic.' The Bystander Effect breaks.

choices.text: Suggest reviewing the rules to the admin
choices.feedback: Structural intervention (rules) prevents recurrence.

steps.speaker: Narrator
steps.text: You are out of the group, but you know the mocking continues. You feel guilty and detached from the community.

choices.text: Send private message to victim: 'I saw the messages, they are not ok.'
choices.feedback: Even if you didn't intervene publicly, private support is vital for the victim.

steps.speaker: Narrator
steps.text: Your action encouraged others to intervene too. The group culture is now clearer and safer for everyone. You have broken pluralistic ignorance.

choices.text: Finish exercise
choices.feedback: An active bystander is the backbone of a healthy community. When one speaks, 'silent disapproval' turns into collective action.
